summary:
Gümüşhane Province stands under the national framework of Turkey, which governs visitors in Gümüşhane. The sources record no provincial legal divergence from that frame in Gümüşhane, so a trans visitor to the province should expect the national pattern of law, document handling and policing rather than any local variant.

Homosexuality has not been treated as a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman Empire's 1858 penal code. Transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, and gender-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988 subject to court-approved procedures.

No comprehensive law in Turkey prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition: the law defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman, which makes same-sex marriage legally impossible though not criminalised, and the gender recorded on a trans person's civil-registry record determines their marriage eligibility.

A leaked omnibus draft known as the 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise LGBT conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' with up to 3 years' imprisonment, criminalise same-sex ceremonies with up to 4 years, raise the age for gender-affirming healthcare to 25 with mandatory infertility and multiple-evaluation conditions, and punish providers with fines and up to 7 years' imprisonment. Fifteen LGBT groups and the national medical association object to the measure. It had not been passed as of that reporting.

Authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, with police using tear gas and water cannons. Amnesty International reported restrictions and excessive force against Pride protesters in 2015 and again in 2024.
tangentialFactors:
The main turbulence in the national framework is legislative rather than judicial: the 11th Judicial Package was still a draft when Human Rights Watch reported it on 29 October 2025, yet its provisions would move LGBT conduct, same-sex ceremonies and gender-affirming healthcare into the penal and civil codes at once, with penalties reaching 7 years for providers.

Objection to that draft comes from inside Turkish civil society and the medical profession: 15 LGBT groups and the national medical association are recorded as opposing it, which indicates organised resistance to the direction of travel rather than an uncontested shift.

The framework a visitor encounters has two layers with different ages. Decriminalisation of homosexuality dates to 1858 and legal gender recognition to 1988, while the anti-discrimination layer does not exist at all, leaving conduct and identity protected on paper in some respects and unprotected in others.

Pride bans have recurred in most years since 2015 across multiple cities, so the pattern of prohibition and force is national in reach rather than confined to a single host city.

Legal gender change has been available in Turkey since 1988, and gender-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988 subject to court-approved procedures, so residents of Gümüşhane access transition through the same court-supervised route as the rest of the country.

The gender recorded on a trans person's civil-registry record determines their marriage eligibility, and marriage is defined by law as a union between a man and a woman. Same-sex marriage is legally impossible though not criminalised, and same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition.

No comprehensive statute prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, so residents have no general statutory claim in employment, services or public accommodation on those grounds.

Residents who take part in Pride events face the national pattern of bans and police force, documented by Amnesty International in 2015 and 2024, rather than any separate provincial permission regime.
